name: SQLite
about: SQLite (E1 in docs/dbaba-curriculum.md). Lab-tested on SQLite 3.53 (Python's sqlite3) and the 3.45 command line: its own error messages (the diagnoser), the other databases' words it refuses with their SQLite rewrites, date arithmetic that runs but means something else (night 1), table designs: type affinity, ids, keys, STRICT tables, foreign keys and ALTER TABLE's limits (night 2), every query rule of nights 1-15 re-checked on SQLite with its own query_rules, wording and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (night 3), and transactions and locking: BEGIN DEFERRED / IMMEDIATE, WAL, busy timeout, savepoints, its transaction errors and the other databases' transaction words (night 4, txn_rules). From night 4 SQLite is no longer notes-only: its answers come from this lab-proven knowledge.

notes.limit: LIMIT n OFFSET m works as on MySQL/PostgreSQL.
notes.concat: || joins text (NULL makes it NULL); CONCAT() exists from 3.44 and skips NULL parts.
notes.full_join: RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN exist only from SQLite 3.39.
notes.now: date('now') / datetime('now') (UTC) or CURRENT_DATE / CURRENT_TIMESTAMP; there is no NOW().
notes.date_add: Dates are text: date(d, '+7 days'), date(d, '+1 month'); no INTERVAL and no DATE_ADD.
notes.date_diff: julianday(end) - julianday(start) gives days (date - date subtracts the leading numbers of the text).
notes.string_agg: group_concat(col, '-') joins a group's text (string_agg is its other name from 3.44).
notes.identity: INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the row id and numbers itself; AUTOINCREMENT only stops ids being reused; INSERT ... RETURNING id (3.35+) gives the new id.
notes.upsert: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(col) DO UPDATE / DO NOTHING (3.24+), like PostgreSQL; also INSERT OR REPLACE / INSERT OR IGNORE.
notes.case: = compares case-sensitively; LIKE ignores case for ASCII letters.
notes.types: Column types are only preferences: an INTEGER column accepted 'hello' and kept it as text. Add CHECK (typeof(col) = 'integer') or a STRICT table (3.37+) to refuse it.
notes.division: int / int drops the fraction (7 / 2 = 3), like PostgreSQL.
notes.greatest: No GREATEST/LEAST: max(a, b, c) / min(a, b, c) with several arguments (NULL if any argument is NULL).
notes.boolean: No BOOLEAN type: TRUE and FALSE are 1 and 0.

SELECT group_concat(x, '-') FROM (SELECT 'a' AS x UNION ALL SELECT 'b')
CREATE TABLE lab_u (n INTEGER); INSERT INTO lab_u VALUES ('hello'); SELECT typeof(n), n FROM lab_u
CREATE TABLE lab_t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT UNIQUE); INSERT INTO lab_t (v) VALUES ('a'); INSERT INTO lab_t (v) VALUES ('a') ON CONFLICT (v) DO NOTHING; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM lab_t

syntax_error:
-- Look just before "{token}": a missing comma, an unclosed ' or (, or words from another database.
-- SQLite has no SHOW TABLES / DESCRIBE (use sqlite_master / PRAGMA table_info), no FOR UPDATE, no INTERVAL, no TOP n (use LIMIT n), no ::casts (use CAST(x AS type)).
-- 'incomplete input' means the statement ends too early: a missing ) or END, or an unclosed quote.
unknown_table: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type IN ('table', 'view') AND name LIKE '%{table_hint}%';

-- Check which FILE the app opened: a wrong or relative path silently creates a new, empty database.
PRAGMA database_list;
unknown_column: -- Text values go in 'single quotes'; "double quotes" are for names.
ambiguous_column:
-- Put the table (or its alias) in front of the column:
SELECT t1.{column}, ... FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON ... WHERE t1.{column} = ...;
unknown_function:
-- SQLite's own words: NOW() -> datetime('now'), CURDATE() -> date('now'), DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY) -> date(d, '+7 days'),
-- DATEDIFF(a, b) -> julianday(a) - julianday(b), YEAR(d) -> strftime('%Y', d), DATE_FORMAT -> strftime, LEFT(s, n) -> substr(s, 1, n),
-- LOCATE / CHARINDEX -> instr(s, x), LEN / CHAR_LENGTH -> length, GREATEST / LEAST -> max(a, b) / min(a, b), NVL / ISNULL -> IFNULL
-- Paste the query and say it is SQLite: I'll rewrite each call.
aggregate_misuse:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000;   -- the condition on the total goes in HAVING

-- In UPDATE/DELETE compare with a subquery:
DELETE FROM t WHERE amount < (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM t);
duplicate_key:
-- See the row that already has it:
SELECT * FROM {table} WHERE {column} = ?;

-- Save without failing when it already exists (upsert, SQLite 3.24+):
INSERT INTO {table} ({column}, ...) VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT ({column}) DO UPDATE SET ... = excluded....;   -- or DO NOTHING
-- INSERT OR REPLACE deletes the old row first: its other columns and its rowid are lost. Prefer the upsert above.
not_null:
-- Send a value for {column} from the app (an empty form field often arrives as NULL),
-- or give the column a DEFAULT: SQLite can't change a column's default with ALTER TABLE, so rebuild the table with it.
fk_missing_parent:
-- Rows that point nowhere, in every table:
PRAGMA foreign_key_check;
bad_value_type:
-- 'datatype mismatch': an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (the rowid) takes only whole numbers; send one, or leave it out for a new id.
-- 'cannot store ... value in ... column': a STRICT table refusing another type; convert it first, e.g. CAST(? AS INTEGER).
value_count_mismatch:
-- Name the columns and give one value for each, in the same order:
INSERT INTO {table} (col1, col2) VALUES (?, ?);

-- See the table's columns in order:
SELECT name FROM pragma_table_info('{table}');
table_exists: SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = '{table}';
disk_full:
-- Space freed by DELETE stays inside the file until (needs free disk about the file's size):
VACUUM;
db_file_locked:
-- Wait for the lock instead of failing at once (milliseconds, per connection):
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;

-- Let readers keep reading while one connection writes:
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
file_readonly:
-- The app's user must be able to write the file AND its folder (SQLite creates a -journal / -wal file next to it):
-- ls -l app.db ; ls -ld <its folder>   then fix the owner or permissions for that user
-- Also check the connection isn't opened read-only (mode=ro in a file: URI).
cannot_open_file:
-- Use an absolute path to a folder that exists and the app can write; a relative path depends on where the app was started.
-- e.g. sqlite3.connect('/srv/app/data/app.db')
file_corrupt:
-- Save what can be read into a new file (sqlite3 command line, 3.29+):
-- sqlite3 broken.db ".recover" | sqlite3 fixed.db
-- 'file is not a database': the path points at another file, or at an encrypted database opened without its key.
alter_not_supported: -- A NOT NULL column can be added with a default: ALTER TABLE {table} ADD COLUMN c TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
strict_type:
-- A STRICT table takes only these type names: INTEGER (or INT), REAL, TEXT, BLOB, ANY.
-- VARCHAR(n) / CHAR(n) -> TEXT (add CHECK (length(col) <= n) to keep the limit), DATE / DATETIME / TIMESTAMP -> TEXT,
-- DECIMAL / NUMERIC / FLOAT / DOUBLE -> REAL (or INTEGER holding paise), BOOLEAN -> INTEGER, JSON -> TEXT, no type -> ANY.
CREATE TABLE {table} (... {column} TEXT ...) STRICT;
-- Or drop STRICT and keep the old type names (then SQLite doesn't enforce them: type affinity).
fk_target_not_key:
-- A foreign key must point at the parent's PRIMARY KEY or a UNIQUE column. Either point it at the key:
--   ... REFERENCES {parent} (id)
-- or make the parent column unique (SQLite: a unique index is enough):
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_{parent}_col ON {parent} (col);
drop_column_blocked:
-- A PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE column can't be dropped at all: rebuild the table without it
-- (CREATE TABLE t_new ..., INSERT INTO t_new SELECT ..., DROP TABLE t, ALTER TABLE t_new RENAME TO t, in one transaction).
statement_still_open:
# Python: read every row first (or close the cursor) before changing the table it reads
rows = conn.execute("SELECT id FROM items").fetchall()
conn.execute("DROP TABLE items_old")

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein :: cast nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use CAST(x AS type), which works on every database.
refuses.fix_hi: CAST(x AS type) likho, ye har database pe chalta hai.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein :: cast nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use CAST(x AS INTEGER).
refuses.fix_hi: CAST(x AS INTEGER) likho.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein :: cast nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use CAST(x AS REAL) for a number with a fraction.
refuses.fix_hi: CAST(x AS REAL) likho.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein :: cast nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use date(x): it gives the YYYY-MM-DD text. (Don't write CAST(x AS DATE) on SQLite: it gives only the year, 2024.)
refuses.fix_hi: date(x) likho (CAST(x AS DATE) SQLite pe sirf saal deta hai).

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein :: cast nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use datetime(x): it gives the YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS text.
refuses.fix_hi: datetime(x) likho.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein :: cast nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use CAST(x AS type) with a type SQLite understands (TEXT, INTEGER, REAL, NUMERIC, BLOB).
refuses.fix_hi: CAST(x AS type) likho (TEXT, INTEGER, REAL, NUMERIC, BLOB).

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein ILIKE nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use LIKE: on SQLite it already ignores case for the letters A-Z (not for letters like é or ा: compare lower() of both, or use a NOCASE column).
refuses.fix_hi: LIKE likho: SQLite pe ye A-Z ke liye pehle se case ignore karta hai.

refuses.title_en: {db} has no DUAL table (that's Oracle / MySQL)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein DUAL table nahi hoti
refuses.fix_en: A SELECT without FROM works on SQLite: drop FROM DUAL.
refuses.fix_hi: FROM DUAL hata do: SQLite pe bina FROM ka SELECT chalta hai.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein SYSDATE nahi hota (wo Oracle ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Use datetime('now') (in UTC; datetime('now', 'localtime') for the computer's local time).
refuses.fix_hi: datetime('now') likho (UTC mein).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no OFFSET ... FETCH (that's SQL Server / Oracle)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein OFFSET ... FETCH nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: SQLite pages with LIMIT n OFFSET m (LIMIT first).
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite mein LIMIT n OFFSET m likho (LIMIT pehle).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no FETCH FIRST (that's the SQL standard / Oracle / SQL Server)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein FETCH FIRST nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: Use LIMIT n at the end of the query.
refuses.fix_hi: Query ke aakhir mein LIMIT n likho.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein SELECT ... FOR UPDATE nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: SQLite locks the whole database file for a write, not rows: start the transaction with BEGIN IMMEDIATE (it takes the write lock at once), then read and write, then COMMIT.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite rows nahi, poori file lock karta hai: transaction BEGIN IMMEDIATE se shuru karo, phir padho-likho, phir COMMIT.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein INSERT IGNORE nahi hota (wo MySQL/MariaDB ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: SQLite says INSERT OR IGNORE. Like INSERT IGNORE it skips rows that break UNIQUE, NOT NULL or CHECK rules, not only duplicates; ON CONFLICT (col) DO NOTHING skips only that conflict.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite mein INSERT OR IGNORE likho (ye bhi duplicate ke alawa NOT NULL / CHECK todne wali rows chhod deta hai).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (that's MySQL/MariaDB)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: SQLite's upsert is ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET, and the new row's values are excluded.col (MySQL's VALUES(col)). Without a column list after ON CONFLICT it needs SQLite 3.35+; name the unique column, ON CONFLICT (email), for older versions.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite ka upsert ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET hai, aur nayi row ki value excluded.col (MySQL ka VALUES(col)).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no VALUES(col) in an upsert (that's MySQL/MariaDB)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein upsert ke andar VALUES(col) nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: The new row's value is excluded.col on SQLite.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite pe nayi row ki value excluded.col hai.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein TRUNCATE nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: DELETE FROM t with no WHERE empties the table (SQLite does it quickly). An AUTOINCREMENT counter keeps counting unless its row in sqlite_sequence is deleted too.
refuses.fix_hi: Bina WHERE ka DELETE FROM t table khaali karta hai.

refuses.to: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' ORDER BY name
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein SHOW TABLES nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: The tables are listed in sqlite_master (the command line also has .tables).
refuses.fix_hi: Tables sqlite_master mein milti hain (command line pe .tables).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no DESCRIBE / SHOW COLUMNS (that's MySQL/MariaDB)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein DESCRIBE nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: PRAGMA table_info(t) lists the columns, their types, NOT NULL, defaults and the key.
refuses.fix_hi: PRAGMA table_info(t) columns dikhata hai.

refuses.error: near the alias or JOIN: syntax error
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein UPDATE ... JOIN nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: Write UPDATE t SET col = ... FROM other WHERE other.key = t.key (SQLite 3.33+), or SET col = (SELECT ... FROM other WHERE other.key = t.key) on older versions.
refuses.fix_hi: UPDATE t SET col = ... FROM other WHERE other.key = t.key likho (SQLite 3.33+).

refuses.error: near the table name: syntax error
refuses.title_en: {db} has no DELETE t FROM t JOIN ... (that's MySQL/MariaDB)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein DELETE t FROM ... JOIN nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: Write DELETE FROM t WHERE key IN (SELECT t.key FROM t JOIN other ON ... WHERE ...).
refuses.fix_hi: DELETE FROM t WHERE key IN (SELECT ...) likho.

refuses.title_en: {db}'s ALTER TABLE can't change a column
refuses.title_hi: {db} ka ALTER TABLE column nahi badal sakta
refuses.fix_en: SQLite's ALTER TABLE renames, adds or drops (3.35+) columns, and from 3.53 sets or drops NOT NULL; nothing else changes a column. To change a type or a default, rebuild the table: CREATE TABLE t_new (...), INSERT INTO t_new SELECT ... FROM t, DROP TABLE t, ALTER TABLE t_new RENAME TO t, all in one transaction with foreign keys off.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite ka ALTER TABLE sirf naam badalta, column jodta ya hataata hai. Type badalne ke liye table dobara banao (nayi table, rows copy, purani drop, rename).

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein REGEXP apne aap nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: SQLite parses REGEXP but has no function behind it unless the app adds one (Python: conn.create_function('regexp', 2, ...)). For simple patterns use LIKE ('a%' starts with a) or GLOB ('[0-9]*' starts with a digit, case-sensitive).
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite mein REGEXP ka function app ko jodna padta hai. Saade patterns ke liye LIKE ya GLOB likho.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein DIV nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: CAST(a / b AS INTEGER) keeps the whole part, toward zero, as DIV does (lab: 7 DIV 2 = 3, -7 DIV 2 = -3 on MariaDB and the rewrite on SQLite).
refuses.fix_hi: CAST(a / b AS INTEGER) likho (DIV ki tarah poora hissa).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no MOD operator word (that's MySQL/MariaDB)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein MOD shabd nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: Use a % b. On SQLite % works on whole numbers (7.5 % 2 is 1.0, not 1.5): for fractions use mod(a, b) where the math functions are built in (3.35+).
refuses.fix_hi: a % b likho (SQLite pe % poore numbers pe chalta hai).

refuses.title_en: {db}'s ALTER TABLE can't add a constraint
refuses.title_hi: {db} ka ALTER TABLE constraint nahi jod sakta
refuses.fix_en: A unique index does the same job and SQLite adds it any time.
refuses.fix_hi: Unique index wahi kaam karta hai aur kabhi bhi jud jaata hai.

refuses.title_hi: {db} ka ALTER TABLE UNIQUE nahi jod sakta
refuses.fix_en: Add a unique index instead (rows that already repeat stop it: 'UNIQUE constraint failed').
refuses.fix_hi: Uski jagah unique index banao.

refuses.title_en: {db} adds an index with CREATE INDEX, not ALTER TABLE
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein index CREATE INDEX se banta hai, ALTER TABLE se nahi
refuses.fix_en: Write it as its own statement.
refuses.fix_hi: Alag statement likho.

refuses.title_en: {db}'s ALTER TABLE can't add a primary key or a foreign key
refuses.title_hi: {db} ka ALTER TABLE primary key ya foreign key nahi jod sakta
refuses.fix_en: Rebuild the table with the key in its CREATE TABLE: PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF; BEGIN; CREATE TABLE t_new (... with the key ...); INSERT INTO t_new SELECT ... FROM t; DROP TABLE t; ALTER TABLE t_new RENAME TO t; PRAGMA foreign_key_check; COMMIT; PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON. (A new column can carry REFERENCES: ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN parent_id INTEGER REFERENCES parent(id).)
refuses.fix_hi: Key ke saath table dobara banao (nayi table, rows copy, purani drop, rename, ek transaction mein). Naya column REFERENCES ke saath jod sakte ho.

refuses.title_en: {db}'s ADD COLUMN has no IF NOT EXISTS
refuses.title_hi: {db} ke ADD COLUMN mein IF NOT EXISTS nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: Check first whether the column is there: SELECT 1 FROM pragma_table_info('t') WHERE name = 'col'; and add it only when that returns nothing.
refuses.fix_hi: Pehle dekho column hai ya nahi (pragma_table_info), na ho tabhi jodo.

refuses.title_en: {db}'s ALTER TABLE adds one column at a time
refuses.title_hi: {db} ka ALTER TABLE ek baar mein ek column jodta hai
refuses.fix_en: Write one ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN ... statement per column.
refuses.fix_hi: Har column ke liye alag ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN likho.

refuses.to: ALTER TABLE \1 ADD COLUMN \2 \3;\nCREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_\1_\2 ON \1 (\2)
refuses.title_hi: {db} UNIQUE column nahi jod sakta
refuses.fix_en: Add the column, then a unique index on it (the old rows get NULL, and NULLs don't clash in a unique index).
refuses.fix_hi: Column jodo, phir uspe unique index (purani rows mein NULL, jo unique index mein takraate nahi).

refuses.error: Cannot add a PRIMARY KEY column
refuses.title_en: {db} can't add a PRIMARY KEY column
refuses.title_hi: {db} PRIMARY KEY column nahi jod sakta
refuses.fix_en: Rebuild the table with the key (CREATE TABLE t_new (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ...); INSERT INTO t_new (...) SELECT ... FROM t; DROP TABLE t; ALTER TABLE t_new RENAME TO t; in one transaction). Every SQLite table already has a rowid you can read meanwhile.
refuses.fix_hi: Key ke saath table dobara banao. Tab tak har SQLite table ka rowid padh sakte ho.

refuses.error: constraint may not be dropped (3.53) / near "CONSTRAINT": syntax error (3.45)
refuses.title_en: {db}'s ALTER TABLE can't drop a constraint
refuses.title_hi: {db} ka ALTER TABLE constraint nahi hata sakta
refuses.fix_en: An index made with CREATE INDEX goes with DROP INDEX name; a key, UNIQUE, CHECK or foreign key written in the CREATE TABLE goes only by rebuilding the table without it (from 3.53, NOT NULL alone: ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c DROP NOT NULL).
refuses.fix_hi: CREATE INDEX wala index DROP INDEX se jaata hai; CREATE TABLE mein likhi key / UNIQUE / CHECK sirf table dobara banake.

refuses.error: Cannot add a column with non-constant default
refuses.title_en: {db} refuses this default when the table already has rows
refuses.title_hi: Table mein rows hon to {db} ye default mana karta hai
refuses.fix_en: ADD COLUMN takes only a fixed default (a number or a text): CURRENT_TIMESTAMP or an expression works on an empty table and fails on one with rows ('Cannot add a column with non-constant default'). Add the column without it, then fill the old rows yourself (preview with SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE col IS NULL first): ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN created_at TEXT; UPDATE t SET created_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE created_at IS NULL. New rows then need the value from the app (or the table rebuilt with the default).
refuses.fix_hi: ADD COLUMN sirf fixed default leta hai: rows wali table pe CURRENT_TIMESTAMP fail hota hai. Bina default jodo, phir purani rows bharo (pehle preview).

refuses.error: Cannot add a NOT NULL column with default value NULL
refuses.title_en: {db} adds a NOT NULL column only with a default
refuses.title_hi: {db} NOT NULL column sirf default ke saath jodta hai
refuses.fix_en: The old rows need a value: on a table with rows this fails ('Cannot add a NOT NULL column with default value NULL'; it works only while the table is empty). Give it a default: ... NOT NULL DEFAULT '' (or 0).
refuses.fix_hi: Purani rows ko value chahiye: rows wali table pe ye fail hota hai. Default do: NOT NULL DEFAULT '' (ya 0).

refuses.title_en: ALTER COLUMN ... SET / DROP NOT NULL needs {db} 3.53 or newer
refuses.title_hi: ALTER COLUMN ... SET / DROP NOT NULL ke liye {db} 3.53+ chahiye
refuses.fix_en: SQLite added it in 3.53.0 (April 2026): lab, 3.53 ran it (and refused SET NOT NULL while a NULL row was there: 'constraint failed'), the 3.45 command line gave a syntax error. Check yours with SELECT sqlite_version(); on an older one, rebuild the table.
refuses.fix_hi: Ye SQLite 3.53.0 (April 2026) mein aaya: lab mein 3.53 ne chalaya, 3.45 ne syntax error diya. SELECT sqlite_version() se dekho; purane pe table dobara banao.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein = ANY (SELECT ...) nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: x = ANY (SELECT c ...) is x IN (SELECT c ...), the same rows.
refuses.fix_hi: x = ANY (...) ko x IN (...) likho, rows wahi.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein <> ALL (SELECT ...) nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: x <> ALL (SELECT c ...) is x NOT IN (SELECT c ...), NULLs included (one NULL in c makes both empty).
refuses.fix_hi: x <> ALL (...) ko x NOT IN (...) likho (NULL ka asar bhi wahi).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no ANY / ALL before a subquery
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein subquery se pehle ANY / ALL nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: Compare with one value instead: x > ANY (SELECT c ...) is x > (SELECT MIN(c) ...), x < ANY is x < (SELECT MAX(c) ...); x > ALL (SELECT c ...) is x > (SELECT MAX(c) ...) and x < ALL is x < (SELECT MIN(c) ...) when c has no NULLs (on an empty subquery ALL is true, so add OR NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...) if that can happen).
refuses.fix_hi: Ek value se tulna karo: > ANY ko > (SELECT MIN(c) ...), > ALL ko > (SELECT MAX(c) ...) likho (c mein NULL na ho).

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein MINUS nahi hota (wo Oracle ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: SQLite says EXCEPT: the rows of the first query that the second doesn't have, without duplicates.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite mein EXCEPT likho.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein LATERAL nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: A subquery in FROM can't see the tables before it on SQLite. Put a correlated subquery in SELECT for one value per row, or use a window function (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)) in a subquery and keep rank 1 for 'the top row per group'.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite mein FROM ki subquery pichhli tables nahi dekhti: SELECT mein correlated subquery, ya ROW_NUMBER() window lagao.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein DISTINCT ON nahi hota (wo PostgreSQL ka hai)

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein START TRANSACTION nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: SQLite starts a transaction with BEGIN (DEFERRED unless you say BEGIN IMMEDIATE, which takes the write lock at once). Every SQLite transaction is SERIALIZABLE, so isolation and READ ONLY words have nothing to set.

refuses.fix_hi: SQLite ki transaction hamesha SERIALIZABLE hai: saadha BEGIN, ya likhna ho to BEGIN IMMEDIATE.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein SET TRANSACTION nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: There is nothing to set: every SQLite transaction is SERIALIZABLE. (PRAGMA read_uncommitted only matters for connections sharing one cache in one process.)
refuses.fix_hi: Set karne ko kuch nahi: SQLite ki har transaction SERIALIZABLE hai.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein SET autocommit nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: SQLite is in autocommit until a BEGIN, and back in it after COMMIT / ROLLBACK: write BEGIN where the transaction starts.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite BEGIN tak autocommit mein hai: jahan transaction shuru ho wahan BEGIN likho.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein SET autocommit nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: COMMIT ends the transaction and SQLite is back in autocommit.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein LOCK TABLES nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: SQLite locks the whole database file, never one table: BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock (readers go on), BEGIN EXCLUSIVE also keeps readers out unless the database is in WAL mode, and COMMIT releases it.
refuses.fix_hi: SQLite poori file lock karta hai, ek table nahi: BEGIN IMMEDIATE write lock leta hai, COMMIT chhodta hai.

refuses.title_hi: {db} mein UNLOCK TABLES nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: The lock ends with the transaction: COMMIT.
refuses.fix_hi: Lock transaction ke saath khatam hota hai: COMMIT.

type_compare.says_en: A column's type is only a preference (its affinity): a literal compared with a column is converted to it, so '2' = 2 finds the row of a TEXT column. An expression (strftime, substr, trim, upper, abs, length ...) has no affinity, so its text is never equal to a number and a number always sorts below any text.
type_compare.lab_en: lab: strftime('%Y', d) = 2024 found 0 of 2 rows, strftime('%Y', d) >= 2025 found all 3, substr(d, 1, 4) = 2024 found 0, abs(n) = '7' found 0, while code = 2 on a TEXT column found its row
lab: code = 2 on a TEXT column holding '2'

date_shape.says_en: SQLite has no date type: dates are text and compare letter by letter, so only 'YYYY-MM-DD' (zero-padded, dashes) sorts like time, and date() / julianday() read only ISO shapes.
date_shape.lab_en: lab: d >= '2024-3-1' found 0 of 2 March-and-later rows, d BETWEEN '2024-1-1' AND '2024-12-31' found 1 of 2, d < '15/06/2024' found 0 of 2, date('2024-1-20') is NULL

pipes.says: On SQLite || joins text (a NULL part makes the whole result NULL).
pipes.says_hi: SQLite pe || text jodta hai (ek hissa NULL ho to poora NULL).

plus_on_text.says: SQLite's + only adds numbers: text that doesn't start with a number counts as 0, with no error or warning ('a' + 'b' = 0, '3' + '4' = 7). || joins text there.
plus_on_text.says_hi: SQLite ka + sirf number jodta hai: text 0 ban jaata hai, bina error ke. Text || se judta hai.

int_division.says: SQLite drops the fraction when both sides are whole numbers (7 / 2 = 3), and a DECIMAL or NUMERIC column holding a whole value stores it as a whole number, so amount / 3 and SUM(amount) / COUNT(*) drop it too.
int_division.says_hi: SQLite pe dono taraf poore number hon to fraction kat jaata hai (7 / 2 = 3); DECIMAL column ki poori value bhi integer rehti hai.
lab: SELECT amount / 3, typeof(amount) FROM t WHERE id = 1
SELECT SUM(amount) / COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE id IN (1, 3)

nulls_in_desc.says_hi: SQLite ASC mein NULL pehle aur DESC mein aakhir mein rakhta hai; NULLS FIRST / LAST se badlo (3.30+).

lab: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY discount, id

nvl.says: SQLite has no NVL (no such function: NVL); IFNULL or COALESCE do the same.

double_quotes.says_hi: SQLite "x" ko pehle column samajhta hai; us naam ka column na ho tabhi text maanta hai. Text single quotes mein likho.

concat_null.says: SQLite's CONCAT (3.44+) skips NULL parts; || makes the whole result NULL.
concat_null.says_hi: SQLite ka CONCAT NULL hisse chhod deta hai (3.44+); || poora NULL kar deta hai.

like_case.says: SQLite's LIKE ignores case for the letters A-Z only ('Asha' LIKE 'asha' is true, 'Äb' LIKE 'äb' is not); GLOB is case-sensitive and uses * and ?.
like_case.says_hi: SQLite ka LIKE sirf A-Z ke liye case nahi dekhta; GLOB case dekhta hai.

update_join.says: SQLite has no JOIN after UPDATE (near "JOIN": syntax error). It writes UPDATE a SET col = ... FROM b WHERE a.x = b.y (3.33+).
update_join.says_hi: SQLite mein UPDATE ke baad JOIN nahi; UPDATE a SET ... FROM b WHERE ... likho (3.33+).
lab: UPDATE t JOIN u ON u.t_id = t.id SET t.name = 'x'

update_from.says: SQLite joins in an UPDATE with UPDATE a SET col = ... FROM b WHERE a.x = b.y (3.33+).
update_from.says_hi: SQLite UPDATE a SET ... FROM b WHERE ... chalata hai (3.33+).
lab:
UPDATE t SET name = u.v FROM u WHERE u.t_id = t.id AND u.id = 3;
SELECT name FROM t WHERE id = 2

set_qualified.says: SQLite refuses a table name on the column being set (near ".": syntax error).
set_qualified.says_hi: SQLite SET mein table ka naam mana karta hai; SET col = ... likho.
lab: UPDATE t SET t.name = 'x' WHERE id = 1

delete_join.says: SQLite has no DELETE a FROM a JOIN b (syntax error); pick the rows with a subquery: DELETE FROM a WHERE key IN (SELECT ...).
delete_join.says_hi: SQLite mein DELETE a FROM a JOIN b nahi; DELETE FROM a WHERE key IN (SELECT ...) likho.
lab: DELETE t FROM t JOIN u ON u.t_id = t.id

delete_using.says: SQLite has no DELETE ... USING (near "USING": syntax error); pick the rows with a subquery: DELETE FROM a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.x = a.y).
delete_using.says_hi: SQLite mein DELETE ... USING nahi; DELETE FROM a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE ...) likho.
lab: DELETE FROM t USING u WHERE u.t_id = t.id

DELETE FROM t WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM u WHERE u.t_id = t.id);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

on_duplicate_key.says: SQLite has no ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (near "DUPLICATE": syntax error); its upsert is ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = excluded.col.
on_duplicate_key.says_hi: SQLite mein ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE nahi; ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = excluded.col likho.
lab: INSERT INTO t (id, name) VALUES (1, 'n') ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE name = 'n'

on_conflict.says: SQLite upserts with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = excluded.col (3.24+); the column list must match a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint, else: ON CONFLICT clause does not match any PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint.
on_conflict.says_hi: SQLite ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = excluded.col chalata hai (3.24+); key UNIQUE honi chahiye.
lab:
INSERT INTO u (id, t_id, v) VALUES (1, 1, 'aa') ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET v = excluded.v;
SELECT v FROM u WHERE id = 1
INSERT INTO t (id, name) VALUES (1, 'n') ON CONFLICT (name) DO NOTHING

lab.error: ON CONFLICT clause does not match any PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint

change_limit.says: Whether SQLite takes ORDER BY / LIMIT on UPDATE or DELETE depends on how it was built (the SQLITE_ENABLE_UPDATE_DELETE_LIMIT option): the lab's Python build of 3.53 refused it (near "ORDER" / "LIMIT": syntax error), Ubuntu's libsqlite3 3.45 ran it. Picking the rows by their rowid runs on every build: ... WHERE rowid IN (SELECT rowid FROM t WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT n).
change_limit.says_hi: SQLite UPDATE/DELETE ke saath LIMIT tabhi leta hai jab wo us option ke saath bana ho (Ubuntu ka haan, lab ka 3.53 nahi). WHERE rowid IN (SELECT rowid FROM t WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT n) har build pe chalta hai.
lab: UPDATE t SET name = 'y' WHERE cat = 1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 1
DELETE FROM t WHERE cat = 1 LIMIT 1

UPDATE t SET name = 'y' WHERE rowid IN (SELECT rowid FROM t WHERE cat = 1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 1);
SELECT id, name FROM t WHERE cat = 1 ORDER BY id

insert_ignore.says: SQLite has no INSERT IGNORE (near "IGNORE": syntax error); it says INSERT OR IGNORE, which also skips rows breaking NOT NULL or CHECK, not only duplicates.
insert_ignore.says_hi: SQLite mein INSERT IGNORE nahi; INSERT OR IGNORE likho.
lab: INSERT IGNORE INTO t (id, name) VALUES (1, 'q')

INSERT OR IGNORE INTO t (id, name) VALUES (1, 'q');
SELECT name FROM t WHERE id = 1

replace_into.says: SQLite accepts REPLACE INTO (another name for INSERT OR REPLACE): when the key exists it deletes the old row and inserts the new one, so the columns not listed go back to their defaults. To change only the listed columns: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET col = excluded.col.
replace_into.says_hi: SQLite REPLACE INTO chalata hai, par purani row hata kar nayi daalta hai: baaki columns default ho jaate hain. Sirf diye columns badalne ke liye ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE.
lab:
REPLACE INTO t (id, name) VALUES (1, 'New');
SELECT name, amount, code FROM t WHERE id = 1

INSERT INTO t (id, name) VALUES (1, 'New') ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET name = excluded.name;
SELECT name, amount, code FROM t WHERE id = 1

join_without_on.says: SQLite runs JOIN, INNER JOIN and even LEFT JOIN without ON as a cross join, with no error (lab: 4 x 3 = 12 rows); write CROSS JOIN when every pair is really wanted.
join_without_on.says_hi: SQLite bina ON ke JOIN (LEFT JOIN bhi) ko cross join bana deta hai, bina error ke (4 x 3 = 12 rows).
lab: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t JOIN u
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t LEFT JOIN u
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t JOIN u ON u.t_id = t.id

star_dup_derived.says: SQLite runs a derived table or CTE whose SELECT * over a join has the same column name twice, renames the second (id:1), and a later id silently means the first one (no 'ambiguous' error).
star_dup_derived.says_hi: SQLite do baar aaye column ka doosra naam badal deta hai (id:1), aur baad mein id chupchaap pehla wala hota hai.
lab: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM t JOIN u ON u.t_id = t.id) AS x ORDER BY 1, 8 LIMIT 1
SELECT id FROM (SELECT * FROM t JOIN u ON u.t_id = t.id) AS x ORDER BY 1
WITH x AS (SELECT * FROM t JOIN u ON u.t_id = t.id) SELECT x.id FROM x ORDER BY 1

union_collation.says: SQLite compares UNION rows with the column's collation, BINARY unless the column says otherwise: 'aarav@mail.test' and 'AARAV@mail.test' stay two rows (a COLLATE NOCASE column makes them one).
union_collation.says_hi: SQLite UNION mein case dekhta hai (BINARY): dono rows alag rehti hain, jab tak column NOCASE na ho.
lab: SELECT email FROM t WHERE id = 1 UNION SELECT email FROM t WHERE id = 2

case_mixed_types.says: SQLite runs it and keeps each result's own type in one column: numbers sort before any text, and a comparison like > 6 is true for every text result ('none' > 6), with no error.
case_mixed_types.says_hi: SQLite chala deta hai aur har value ka apna type rakhta hai: number text se pehle sort hote hain, aur text har number se bada maana jaata hai.
lab: SELECT id, CASE WHEN discount IS NULL THEN 'none' ELSE discount END AS d FROM t ORDER BY d, id
SELECT id FROM t WHERE CASE WHEN discount IS NULL THEN 'none' ELSE discount END > 6 ORDER BY id

text_vs_number.says: SQLite turns the number into text to compare it with a TEXT column (the column's type decides), so the index is used (lab: SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX), but '098' doesn't equal 98, and < / > compare letter by letter ('7' > '50').
text_vs_number.says_hi: SQLite number ko text bana kar TEXT column se milata hai: index chalta hai, par '098' 98 ke barabar nahi aur < / > akshar-dar-akshar.
lab: SELECT id FROM t WHERE code = 98
SELECT id FROM t WHERE code < 50 ORDER BY id
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE code = 98
SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX t_code (code=?)

row_comparison.says: (a, b) > (x, y) works on SQLite (3.15+), a NULL makes it not TRUE, and an index on (a, b) serves it (lab: SEARCH ... ((cat,rowid)>(?,?))).
row_comparison.says_hi: SQLite (a, b) > (x, y) chalata hai (3.15+) aur index use karta hai.
lab: SELECT id FROM t WHERE (cat, id) > (1, 1) ORDER BY id
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE (cat, id) > (1, 1) ORDER BY cat, id
SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX t_cat ((cat,rowid)>(?,?))

window_needs_order.says: SQLite runs them without ORDER BY, but every row is a tie: RANK() gives 1 to every row and LAG/LEAD take whatever row came before.
window_needs_order.says_hi: SQLite bina ORDER BY chala deta hai, par RANK() sabko 1 deta hai aur LAG/LEAD koi bhi row lete hain.
lab: SELECT DISTINCT RANK() OVER () FROM t
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT LAG(id) OVER () AS p FROM t) WHERE p IS NULL

recursion_limit.says: SQLite has no round limit for a recursive WITH: it keeps going until the query is interrupted or memory runs out (lab: 5000 rounds ran, no limit).
recursion_limit.says_hi: SQLite recursive WITH ko rokta nahi: wo tab tak chalta hai jab tak rok na diya jaaye.
lab: WITH RECURSIVE n(x) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5000) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM n

recursive_text_width.says: SQLite gives text no fixed width, so a recursive part that makes the anchor's text longer runs fine (lab: CAST('x' AS VARCHAR(1)) grew to 9 letters).
recursive_text_width.says_hi: SQLite text ki lambai fix nahi karta, isliye recursive hissa text lamba kar sakta hai.
lab: WITH RECURSIVE p(n, s) AS (SELECT 1, CAST('x' AS VARCHAR(1)) UNION ALL SELECT n + 1, s || 'yy' FROM p WHERE n < 5) SELECT MAX(length(s)) FROM p

volatile_once.says: random() written twice gives two values per row on SQLite, and neither a subquery in FROM, nor a plain WITH, nor the SELECT name used in WHERE helps, because SQLite works each copy out again (lab: about a quarter of 300 rows passed 'r < 0 AND r >= 0' in all three forms); only WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED (3.35+) keeps one value per row.
volatile_once.says_hi: SQLite pe random() do baar likha to har row ke do alag value; FROM ki subquery ya saada WITH bhi nahi bachata, sirf WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED.
lab: SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 FROM g WHERE random() < 0 AND random() >= 0
SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 FROM (SELECT * FROM (SELECT random() AS r FROM g) AS x WHERE r < 0 AND r >= 0)
SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 FROM (SELECT random() AS r FROM g WHERE r < 0 AND r >= 0)
WITH x AS (SELECT random() AS r FROM g) SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 FROM x WHERE r < 0 AND r >= 0
WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT random() AS r FROM g) SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 FROM x WHERE r < 0 AND r >= 0

skip_locked.says: SQLite has no FOR UPDATE, SKIP LOCKED or NOWAIT (near "FOR": syntax error): one writer at a time holds the whole database, so a job queue claims a job with UPDATE jobs SET taken_by = ? WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE taken_by IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 1) RETURNING id inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE.
skip_locked.says_hi: SQLite mein FOR UPDATE / SKIP LOCKED nahi: ek samay ek hi writer; BEGIN IMMEDIATE ke andar UPDATE ... RETURNING se job lo.
lab: SELECT id FROM t FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

lock_scan.says: SQLite locks the whole database file for a write, not rows: while one connection writes, others can read (in WAL mode) but every other writer waits or gets 'database is locked'.
lock_scan.says_hi: SQLite likhte waqt poori database file lock karta hai, rows nahi.

gap_locks.says: SQLite takes no row or gap locks: a write transaction holds the whole database, so there is nothing in between to lock.
gap_locks.says_hi: SQLite row ya gap lock nahi leta: poori file ek writer ke paas.

deadlock.says: SQLite has no deadlock error: two connections that both read and then try to write get 'database is locked' (SQLITE_BUSY) for one of them; BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock up front so that can't happen.
deadlock.says_hi: SQLite mein deadlock error nahi, 'database is locked' aata hai; BEGIN IMMEDIATE se pehle hi write lock lo.

like_prefix_index.says: SQLite's LIKE ignores case, so an ordinary (BINARY) index can't serve LIKE 'abc%' (lab: SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX, every entry read). An index made with COLLATE NOCASE, PRAGMA case_sensitive_like = ON, or GLOB 'abc*' (case-sensitive) turn it into a range (lab: SEARCH ... (name>? AND name<?)).
like_prefix_index.says_hi: SQLite ka LIKE case nahi dekhta, isliye saada index LIKE 'abc%' mein kaam nahi aata; COLLATE NOCASE index ya GLOB 'abc*' se range banti hai.
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE name LIKE 'As%'
SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX t_name
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE name GLOB 'As*'
SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX t_name (name>? AND name<?)

expression_index.says: SQLite indexes an expression directly (3.9+): CREATE INDEX t_lower_email ON t (lower(email)); WHERE lower(email) = ... then uses it (lab: SEARCH ... (<expr>=?)).
expression_index.says_hi: SQLite expression pe seedha index banata hai: CREATE INDEX ... ON t (lower(email)).
lab:
CREATE INDEX t_lower ON t (lower(email));
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE lower(email) = 'm@x.test'
SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX t_lower (<expr>=?)

optimizer_sargable.says: SQLite doesn't turn a function on a column (strftime, substr, date) into a range by itself: the index is only scanned end to end (lab: SCAN), while created >= '2024-01-01' AND created < '2025-01-01' is a SEARCH.
optimizer_sargable.says_hi: SQLite column pe function ko range nahi banata: poora index padhta hai; seedhi range likho.
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE substr(name, 1, 2) = 'As'
SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX t_name
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE name >= 'As' AND name < 'At'
SEARCH t USING COVERING INDEX t_name (name>? AND name<?)

or_same_table.says: SQLite can use two indexes for an OR on one table (EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: MULTI-INDEX OR, one SEARCH per index).
or_same_table.says_hi: SQLite OR ke liye do index use kar sakta hai (MULTI-INDEX OR).
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE name = 'Asha' OR code = '7'

offset_reads.says: SQLite reads and throws away every skipped row for OFFSET (EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows a plain SCAN); keyset paging (WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n) starts at the right place.
offset_reads.says_hi: SQLite OFFSET ki har chhodi row padhta hai; WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n tez hai.
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE id > 2 ORDER BY id LIMIT 2
SEARCH t USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid>?)

repeated_subquery.says: SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows one CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY per copy: each copy runs for every row.
repeated_subquery.says_hi: SQLite har copy ko har row ke liye alag chalata hai (CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY).
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM u WHERE u.t_id = t.id) FROM t ORDER BY (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM u WHERE u.t_id = t.id)
SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX t_cat
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY

same_subquery.says: SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows one SCALAR SUBQUERY per copy (each worked out once, but each on its own).
same_subquery.says_hi: SQLite har copy ko alag SCALAR SUBQUERY banata hai.
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM t) AND discount < (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM t)

cte_read_twice.says: SQLite builds a CTE that is read twice once (EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: MATERIALIZE) and doesn't push a filter on one use into it, so the whole CTE is made first.
cte_read_twice.says_hi: SQLite do baar padhe CTE ko ek baar banata hai (MATERIALIZE) aur filter andar nahi le jaata.
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN WITH x AS (SELECT cat, COUNT(*) AS n FROM t GROUP BY cat) SELECT * FROM x a JOIN x b ON a.cat = b.cat WHERE a.cat = 1
SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX t_cat
SEARCH b USING AUTOMATIC PARTIAL COVERING INDEX (cat=?)

exists_to_in.says: SQLite runs IN (SELECT ...) as a list it builds once. A correlated EXISTS on a column with no index depends on the version: 3.53 built an automatic index for it (AUTOMATIC PARTIAL COVERING INDEX), 3.45 ran it as a CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY that scans the table for every outer row. Both give the same rows when there are no NULLs; an index on the linked column makes both a SEARCH.
exists_to_in.says_hi: SQLite IN aur EXISTS dono ko theek se chalata hai; NULL na ho to rows same.
lab: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE id IN (SELECT t_id FROM u)
SEARCH t USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM t WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM u WHERE u.t_id = t.id)
SCAN t USING COVERING INDEX t_cat
SEARCH u EXISTS USING AUTOMATIC PARTIAL COVERING INDEX (t_id=?)

scalar_subquery_rows.says: SQLite takes the first row a scalar subquery returns and ignores the rest, with no error (lab: id = (SELECT t_id FROM u) matched only 1, though u links to 1 and 2).
scalar_subquery_rows.says_hi: SQLite subquery ki pehli row le leta hai aur baaki chhod deta hai, bina error ke.
lab: SELECT id FROM t WHERE id = (SELECT t_id FROM u ORDER BY id DESC) ORDER BY id
SELECT id FROM t WHERE id IN (SELECT t_id FROM u) ORDER BY id

division_by_zero.says: SQLite gives NULL for x / 0 and x % 0, with no error.
division_by_zero.says_hi: SQLite x / 0 pe NULL deta hai, bina error ke.

union_part_order.says: SQLite refuses ORDER BY or LIMIT inside a UNION part (ORDER BY clause should come after UNION not before); one ORDER BY / LIMIT at the end sorts the whole result, or wrap the part: SELECT * FROM (SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT n).
union_part_order.says_hi: SQLite UNION ke hisse mein ORDER BY / LIMIT mana karta hai; ek ORDER BY aakhir mein, ya hissa subquery mein lapeto.
lab: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id UNION SELECT id FROM u

lab.error: ORDER BY clause should come after UNION not before

lab: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT 1) UNION SELECT id FROM u ORDER BY 1

offset_alone.says: SQLite needs LIMIT before OFFSET (near "OFFSET": syntax error); LIMIT -1 OFFSET n means 'all the rest'.
offset_alone.says_hi: SQLite mein OFFSET se pehle LIMIT chahiye; LIMIT -1 OFFSET n ka matlab baaki sab.
lab: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id OFFSET 2
SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id LIMIT -1 OFFSET 2

cast_prefix.says: SQLite's CAST to a number reads the leading number and drops the rest, with no error: CAST('12abc' AS INTEGER) = 12, CAST('x' AS REAL) = 0.0.
cast_prefix.says_hi: SQLite CAST shuru ka number padhta hai aur baaki chhod deta hai: '12abc' -> 12, 'x' -> 0.
lab: SELECT CAST('12abc' AS INTEGER), CAST('1.9' AS INTEGER), CAST('x' AS REAL)

recursive_keyword.says: SQLite runs a WITH that reads itself even without the word RECURSIVE (other databases need it; writing it is harmless).
recursive_keyword.says_hi: SQLite RECURSIVE likhe bina bhi khud ko padhne wala WITH chala deta hai.
lab: WITH n(x) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 3) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM n

schema_rules.about: How SQLite takes a CREATE TABLE (E1 night 2): a type name only gives a column its affinity, a few things look like other databases' rules but aren't checked, and some of their words are refused. Lab: SQLite 3.53 (Python's sqlite3) and the 3.45 command line.

affinity.says: The declared type is read for these letters in this order: INT -> INTEGER; CHAR, CLOB or TEXT -> TEXT; BLOB or no type -> BLOB; REAL, FLOA or DOUB -> REAL; anything else (DECIMAL, DATE, DATETIME, BOOLEAN, STRING, JSON) -> NUMERIC.

rowid_alias.says: Only a single-column PRIMARY KEY whose declared type is exactly INTEGER (any case, no length, not DESC, not in a WITHOUT ROWID table) becomes the rowid and numbers itself. INT, BIGINT, INTEGER(11), SERIAL, UNSIGNED INTEGER and 'INT AUTO_INCREMENT' are ordinary columns: leave them out of an INSERT and the id is NULL, and NULL ids don't clash, so the key keeps nothing unique.
lab: id INT PRIMARY KEY, two INSERTs without id
id INTEGER(11) / BIGINT / SERIAL / UNSIGNED INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
AUTOINCREMENT is only allowed on an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
INT PRIMARY KEY in a STRICT table, INSERT without id

pk_null.says: Any other PRIMARY KEY (TEXT, two columns, INT) accepts NULL in an ordinary table, and NULLs never clash; NOT NULL on the key's columns, STRICT or WITHOUT ROWID stop it.
lab: code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, two INSERTs without code
the same with NOT NULL, STRICT or WITHOUT ROWID

unenforced.says: VARCHAR(n), CHAR(n) and UNSIGNED are accepted and not checked: the length is not a limit and CHAR is not padded.

no_date_type.says: There is no date type: DATE, DATETIME and TIMESTAMP give NUMERIC affinity, so anything goes in and the shape decides how it sorts. CHECK (d IS date(d)) keeps one day shape ('YYYY-MM-DD'); CHECK (t IS datetime(t)) keeps 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP passes; a 'T' or fractions don't).
lab: CHECK (t IS datetime(t)) with DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, and NULL
'2024-03-01' (rolled over, so the CHECK sees a different value)

money.says: There is no exact decimal type: DECIMAL / NUMERIC keep 1.10 as the binary REAL 1.1, the same as REAL, FLOAT and DOUBLE. Exact money is a whole number of the smallest unit (paise / cents) in INTEGER.

strict.says: A STRICT table (3.37+) takes only INT, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and ANY, and refuses a value that can't be converted without loss.
lab: cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column u.i

foreign_keys.says: FOREIGN KEY and REFERENCES are stored but checked only on connections that run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (off by default). The parent may be created later, nothing indexes the child column, a link to a column that is not a key makes every write to the child fail once checking is on, and the two ends' types are not compared.
lab: the same with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
accepted, and works once the parent exists
none; EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: SCAN c
REFERENCES p(code), code not unique, foreign_keys on, INSERT

schema_rules.reserved_note: Lab (3.53): these were refused as a bare column or table name (near "x": syntax error); user, desc, key, range, rows, end, offset, window, date, status, type and name were accepted.

foreign_syntax.says: Words from MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL table scripts that SQLite refuses (lab: syntax errors): AUTO_INCREMENT after PRIMARY KEY, GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY, ENGINE= / CHARSET= / COLLATE= / AUTO_INCREMENT= table options, ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, KEY / INDEX / UNIQUE KEY inside CREATE TABLE, ENUM(...), DEFAULT now(). Accepted without meaning: backticks, UNSIGNED, TEXT[], JSONB (text), TIMESTAMPTZ (NUMERIC).

query_lab_setup: CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, amount DECIMAL(10,2), discount DECIMAL(10,2), code VARCHAR(10), cat INT, email TEXT)
CREATE TABLE u (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, t_id INT, v TEXT)
CREATE TABLE g (i INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 300) INSERT INTO g SELECT i FROM n

wording.to: SQLite stops with 'sub-select returns N columns - expected 1'
SQLite 'sub-select returns N columns - expected 1' deta hai

wording.to: so when one outer row has two of them SQLite silently shows the first it finds, with no error (lab: one value of the two)

wording.re: isliye do milte hi MySQL/MariaDB error 1242 aur PostgreSQL 21000
wording.to: isliye do milne pe SQLite chupchaap pehli wali dikha deta hai, bina error

wording.to: SQLite never stops (it has no round limit)

wording.to: (SQLite has no CYCLE clause)

(SQLite: has N values for M columns)

wording.to: SQLite stops with 'duplicate WITH table name'
(SQLite: duplicate WITH table name)

wording.to: SQLite stops with 'misuse of window function'
(SQLite: misuse of window function)

wording.to: SQLite stops with 'misuse of aliased window function \1'

wording.to: SQLite refuses it ('misuse of aggregate function')
SQLite 'misuse of aggregate function' deta hai

wording.to: SQLite stops with 'misuse of aggregate function'

txn_rules.about: How SQLite reads a transaction script (E1 night 4, app/agents/sqltxn.py): each lab line is a script run by tests/practice/txnlab.py (autocommit, one connection, then what is saved read from a second one) and run again by tests/practice/test_e1_sqlite4.py.

nested_begin.error: cannot start a transaction within a transaction
nested_begin.says: SQLite refuses a second BEGIN while one is open ('cannot start a transaction within a transaction'); what follows still runs inside the first transaction, so a ROLLBACK then undoes all of it (lab).
nested_begin.says_hi: SQLite khuli transaction mein doosra BEGIN mana karta hai ('cannot start a transaction within a transaction'); baaki statements pehli transaction mein hi chalte hain, ROLLBACK sab wapas leta hai.

errors: cannot start a transaction within a transaction

end_without_begin.error: cannot commit - no transaction is active / cannot rollback - no transaction is active
end_without_begin.says: With no BEGIN, SQLite saved each statement as it ran; COMMIT / ROLLBACK then fail with 'cannot commit - no transaction is active' / 'cannot rollback - no transaction is active', and the ROLLBACK undoes nothing (lab). Python's sqlite3 module (unless autocommit is on) opens a transaction itself before INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE, so there it does end one.
end_without_begin.says_hi: BEGIN ke bina SQLite har statement chalte hi save kar deta hai; phir COMMIT / ROLLBACK 'no transaction is active' dete hain aur ROLLBACK kuch wapas nahi karta. (Python ka sqlite3 khud INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE se pehle transaction kholta hai.)
lab:
UPDATE lab_tx SET v = 11 WHERE id = 1;
ROLLBACK;

errors: cannot rollback - no transaction is active

lab:
UPDATE lab_tx SET v = 11 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

errors: cannot commit - no transaction is active

ddl_commits.says: SQLite keeps CREATE / ALTER / DROP inside the transaction: ROLLBACK undoes them too (lab).
ddl_commits.says_hi: SQLite mein CREATE / ALTER / DROP transaction ke andar rehte hain: ROLLBACK unhe bhi wapas leta hai.

outside_only.error: cannot VACUUM from within a transaction / cannot change into wal mode from within a transaction
outside_only.says: VACUUM and a change of journal_mode refuse to run inside a transaction ('cannot VACUUM from within a transaction', 'cannot change into wal mode from within a transaction'); the rest of the transaction carries on (lab). Run VACUUM after COMMIT and set the journal mode before BEGIN.
outside_only.says_hi: VACUUM aur journal_mode badalna transaction ke andar mana hai; VACUUM COMMIT ke baad, journal mode BEGIN se pehle.

errors: cannot VACUUM from within a transaction
cannot change into wal mode from within a transaction

savepoint_missing.says: SQLite stops at a RELEASE / ROLLBACK TO of a name that was never made ('no such savepoint: name'); the transaction stays open and goes on (lab).
savepoint_missing.says_hi: Jo savepoint bana hi nahi uska RELEASE / ROLLBACK TO SQLite mana karta hai ('no such savepoint').

savepoint_outside.says: On SQLite a SAVEPOINT outside a transaction starts one, and RELEASE of it commits (lab); ROLLBACK TO keeps it open.
savepoint_outside.says_hi: SQLite mein transaction ke bahar SAVEPOINT nayi transaction shuru karta hai; uska RELEASE commit karta hai.

left_open.says: The transaction stays open: SQLite keeps the whole database locked for every other writer ('database is locked') until it ends, and closing the connection rolls it back (lab: nothing was saved).
left_open.says_hi: Transaction khuli reh jaati hai: jab tak khatam na ho, SQLite poori database ko baaki writers ke liye lock rakhta hai ('database is locked'); connection band hone pe rollback.
lab:
BEGIN;
UPDATE lab_tx SET v = 19 WHERE id = 1;

deferred_upgrade.says: A plain BEGIN (DEFERRED) takes no lock until its first read, and only a read lock then; its first write must upgrade to the write lock, and if another connection wrote in between, that write fails at once with 'database is locked' (SQLITE_BUSY, or SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT in WAL mode); a busy timeout does not make it wait (lab: it failed after 0.00 s with a 3-second timeout, in both journal modes). BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock at the start, where the busy timeout does wait (lab: it waited about 0.5 s and went through).
deferred_upgrade.says_hi: Saadha BEGIN pehle sirf read lock leta hai; baad ka write lock upgrade karta hai, aur beech mein kisi aur ne likha to turant 'database is locked' (busy timeout bhi nahi rukwata). BEGIN IMMEDIATE shuru mein hi write lock leta hai, wahan timeout intezaar karata hai.
lab: two connections, rollback journal: A BEGIN; SELECT; (B holds BEGIN IMMEDIATE + UPDATE, commits after 0.5 s); A UPDATE with busy timeout 3 s
two connections, WAL: A BEGIN; SELECT; B UPDATE (commits); A UPDATE
the same with A BEGIN IMMEDIATE (busy timeout 3 s)

no_txn_writes.says: With no BEGIN, SQLite saves each change on its own: if a later one fails, the earlier ones stay (lab), and each one waits for its own disk sync (lab: 500 single-row INSERTs took about 0.5 s one by one and 0.002 s inside one BEGIN ... COMMIT). Inside a transaction a failed statement is undone alone and the transaction goes on: ROLLBACK on the error to undo the rest (lab: COMMIT kept the change before the error).
no_txn_writes.says_hi: BEGIN ke bina SQLite har badlav alag save karta hai: baad wala fail ho to pehle wale reh jaate hain, aur har ek apna disk sync leta hai (500 INSERT: 0.5 s alag-alag, 0.002 s ek transaction mein).
